families.s: HSE slips-and-trips prevention in educational premises
families.t: busy circulation, running, carried loads, footwear, lighting, contamination, obstructions, cleaning, flooring and public access
f: Slips and trips are the most common cause of injury at work and a major reported injury to the public.
Education sites can have large numbers of staff, pupils, students and visitors moving at the same time.
Running or carrying awkward items can increase risk.
Poor lighting can obscure uneven surfaces and changes in level.
Water, food and litter can contaminate floors.
Bags and trailing cables are common obstructions.
Cleaning regimes should identify problem areas and avoid leaving unsafe surfaces.
Slip-resistant flooring or footwear may be needed in areas such as kitchens and food service.
families.g: Education slip risk depends on circulation and occupancy, floor and contamination, cleaning and drying, footwear, lighting, bags and cables, stairs and levels, supervision and maintenance.

families.s: HSE proportionate planning and management of school trips
families.t: real risks, planning, authorisation, everyday risks, serious breaches, precautions, providers, licensing and incident learning
f: School visits should focus on managing real risks rather than excessive paperwork.
Planning and authorisation should be proportionate to the activity and hazards.
Everyday-risk visits can use simpler planning arrangements.
Sensible precautions should not prevent valuable off-site learning.
An accident does not by itself prove a breach of health and safety law.
HSE attention is directed to serious failures and significant real risks.
Providers of specified adventure activities may require licensing.
Schools should review arrangements after incidents, near misses or material changes to the visit.
families.g: School-trip risk depends on activity and location, participants and supervision, transport and provider, weather and environment, emergency arrangements, competence and proportionate planning.

families.s: HSE individual risk assessment for disabled pupils and pupils with SEN or ASN
families.t: individual needs, equality, reasonable adjustments, carers, communication, behaviour, treatment, infection, transport and review
f: Education employers should not assume that all disabled pupils create additional health and safety risk.
Specific risks should be assessed individually rather than through blanket policies.
Health and safety duties should be balanced with equality duties and access to education.
Reasonable adjustments can enable participation while controlling risk.
Employees, pupils and carers should be involved in identifying needs and precautions.
Assessment may need to consider behaviour, communication, treatment, infection, mobility and transport.
Information about individual needs should be sought before attendance where practicable.
Arrangements should be reviewed because a pupil's needs can change over time.
families.g: SEN/ASN risk depends on individual capability and communication, activity and environment, equipment and assistance, behaviour and treatment, transport, staff competence, equality adjustments and review.

families.s: HSE moving and handling of disabled pupils and pupils with SEN or ASN
families.t: transfers, slide sheets, hoists, wheelchairs, posture, floor recovery, behaviour, space, care plans, equipment maintenance and staffing
f: Health and safety law does not prohibit all moving and handling of pupils.
Employers should use a risk-management approach that enables participation.
Individual care plans should identify the correct equipment and moves.
Slide sheets, transfer boards, hoists, turntables and suitable chairs can reduce handling risk.
Floor recovery after a fall or emergency should be planned.
Wheelchairs and mobility aids should be maintained so they move safely.
Assessment should consider behaviour, communication, weight-bearing ability, space, floors and lighting.
The number and competence of staff available for the task should be considered.
families.g: Education moving-and-handling risk depends on pupil needs and behaviour, transfer and emergency task, equipment and maintenance, space and floor, staff capability and number, care plan, communication and supervision.

families.s: HSE RIDDOR incident reporting guidance for schools
families.t: employees, pupils, visitors, school trips, work activity, reportability, dangerous occurrences, records, investigation and proportionality
f: HSE provides school-specific guidance on how RIDDOR applies to accidents, diseases and dangerous occurrences.
Most incidents in schools or on school trips do not need to be reported to HSE.
Reportability depends on the event, the person affected and its connection with work activity.
Specified employee injuries and occupational diseases may be reportable.
Some injuries to pupils or visitors are reportable where they arise from a work-related accident and meet the reporting criteria.
Specified dangerous occurrences may be reportable even where no one is injured.
Schools should keep suitable records and investigate incidents to identify control failures.
Internal recording and learning may be appropriate even where an event is not RIDDOR-reportable.
families.g: School incident-reporting duty depends on who was affected, injury or event type, work connection, treatment and outcome, timing, legal criteria, records and investigation findings.
